title: India — priest jailed 18 years for abusing four minor seminarians (Kollam)
who: Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate (St Eugene de Mazenod congregation); Diocese of Punalur
what: On 29 April 2022 the Kollam POCSO court sentenced Fr Thomas Parekkulam, 35, to 18 years (consecutive terms in four cases) and a Rs 1 lakh fine for sexually abusing four minor seminarians, Class 12 students living with him in a rented house in 2017. The case was registered after one boy contacted Childline. The boys left the seminary.

title: Pakistan — Karachi madrassa cleric jailed for abusing two boys
who: Madrassa in Landhi, Karachi
what: A Karachi sessions court gave madrassa teacher Qari Muhammad Anwar two concurrent 15-year sentences and Rs 1 million fines in each case for sexually abusing a 13-year-old and a 17-year-old student in a room at the madrassa, under threat. Cases were registered in 2025 after the younger boy told his parents he and other students had been abused; the older boy came forward after seeing TV reports.

title: Bangladesh — Chattogram Quran academy director jailed for life
who: Rahmania Tahfizul Quran Academy (madrasa)
what: On 4 June 2025 Chattogram's Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal-7 sentenced Nazim Uddin, 41, director and teacher of a Quran memorisation academy, to imprisonment until death and a Tk 500,000 fine for raping and sexually assaulting six minor students between 15 August 2019 and 1 March 2021. The case was filed on 4 March 2021 by a victim's brother; he confessed in court.

title: Uganda — Anglican priest jailed 28 years for defiling a 12-year-old
who: Church of Uganda (Anglican)
what: The High Court sitting in Bushenyi, under Justice Joyce Kavuma, sentenced Rev. Muhwezi Gordon, 46, a priest at Nyarutuntu Church of Uganda in Mitooma district, to 28 years for aggravated defilement of a 12-year-old girl in May 2021.

title: Cameroon — Bertoua parish priest detained over rape of a minor servant
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Bertoua
what: On 19 May 2022 a 47-year-old Catholic parish priest in Bertoua was placed in pre-trial detention on charges of corrupting youth, rape of a minor and transmitting a contagious disease, after the parents of his former house servant complained that he had abused her for about four years from age 14. A prosecutor's warrant was issued on 12 May.

title: Guatemala — priest sentenced to 16 years 7 months for raping a 14-year-old
who: Catholic Church in Guatemala
what: On 18 September 2018 a Guatemalan court sentenced priest Ignacio López to 16 years and 7 months for raping a 14-year-old girl whom he met when she attended church to prepare for her first communion.

title: Zambia — Grace Ministries pastor convicted of defiling a 12-year-old
who: Grace Ministries, Shibuyunji
what: The Lusaka Magistrates' Court convicted Wycliff Kamando, 60, pastor of Grace Ministries in Shibuyunji, of defiling a 12-year-old girl between 3 January and 8 April 2024; he faced a mandatory minimum of 15 years. The magistrate said he had abused his role as a spiritual leader.

title: Zambia — Kabwata Presbyterian minister convicted of defiling his niece
who: Presbyterian church, Kabwata, Lusaka
what: A Lusaka magistrate convicted Reverend Allan Muchulu, a preacher at Kabwata Presbyterian church, of repeatedly defiling his 11-year-old niece who lived with him from 2020; he was arrested in March 2023 after she confided in her aunt, and was committed to the High Court for sentencing of at least 18 years.

title: Afghanistan — students report sexual abuse in Taliban-run madrasahs
who: Taliban-run madrasah system (6,836 male madrasahs per a Feb 2024 UN report)
cover_up: A 16-year-old said he reported a teacher to the school's qari, who only told the teacher to stop; the teacher admitted it and continued. The schools are run by the de facto Taliban authorities.
what: In March 2024 RFE/RL's Radio Azadi published accounts from male students aged 10 to 17 at Taliban-run madrasahs in western and southwestern Afghanistan who said teachers pressured them and classmates into sexual acts and used corporal punishment; some left school. The report cited a February 2024 UN report counting 6,836 Taliban-established madrasahs for boys and a decree seeking 100,000 new madrasah teachers.

title: Afghanistan — rape of a 10-year-old girl at an unregistered Badghis madrasah
who: Imam Asem madrasah (unregistered)
what: On 26 December 2019 a girl believed to be 10 was raped in the washroom of the Imam Asem madrasah in Qala-e Naw. Badghis security chief Sher Aqa Alekozai said 18 students of the school were arrested while investigators tried to identify the perpetrator. The Education Ministry said the madrasah was not registered, as required; Afghanistan then had over 1,000 registered madrasahs and many operated with little or no government supervision.

title: Ghana — Shiva Linga Church head pastor jailed for defiling eight girls
who: Shiva Linga Church, Ghana branch
cover_up: Charged in 2007, he jumped bail after four witnesses had testified and hid for four years, based in Abidjan, until journalist Anas Aremeyaw Anas helped locate him in Techiman.
what: An Accra Fast Track High Court sentenced Nana Akwesi Agyemang, head pastor of the Ghana branch of Shiva Linga Church, to 15 years on eight counts of defiling girls whom parents had sent to live at his residence near Dome through his church work. One girl had come from Abidjan. Parents protested that the sentence was too light.

title: Ghana — prayer-camp pastor jailed 20 years for defiling a 15-year-old
who: Jesus Faith Tabernacle Prayer Centre
what: A Circuit Court at Akim Swedru sentenced Paul Nkansah, head pastor of a prayer camp at Akim Achiase, to 20 years for defiling a 15-year-old schoolgirl visiting her sick mother at the camp, after claiming she needed 'deliverance' and drugging her.

title: Ferns Report — Diocese of Ferns
who: Catholic Diocese of Ferns
cover_up: Bishop Herlihy moved accused priests to other posts or dioceses for a period, then reinstated them; Gardaí failed to record or properly investigate some pre-1988 complaints
what: The state Ferns Inquiry, published 25 October 2005, examined more than 100 allegations of child sexual abuse made between 1962 and 2002 against 21 priests of the diocese. Bishop Donal Herlihy moved accused priests temporarily and then reinstated them, and ordained men he knew or should have known posed a risk. Bishop Brendan Comiskey never got a priest to stand aside from ministry. The report found Garda handling of one of eight formal complaints 'wholly inadequate' and some pre-1988 complaints were not recorded.

title: Murphy Report — Archdiocese of Dublin
who: Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin
cover_up: Abuse 'covered up' 1975–2004; bishops generally did not report to Gardaí before 1996; archdiocese took out insurance against abuse litigation from 1987; Gardaí knew of complaints against Fr Tony Walsh in 1990–91 and took no action
what: The Commission of Investigation into the Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin reported on 26 November 2009. It examined a representative sample of 46 priests out of 102 within its remit; 320 people complained of child sexual abuse between 1975 and 2004. It found former Archbishops McQuaid, Ryan, McNamara and Connell failed to report what they knew to the Gardaí, and said the archdiocese's move to take out insurance against abuse claims showed it knew abuse was a potential major cost. It also criticised the Gardaí for treating priests as outside their remit; the Garda Commissioner called the report 'difficult and disturbing reading'.

title: Cloyne Report — Diocese of Cloyne
who: Catholic Diocese of Cloyne; Bishop John Magee
cover_up: Nine complaints that should have gone to the Gardaí were not reported; none of the 1996–2008 complaints reported to the health service; Vatican's reaction to Irish guidelines described as 'entirely unhelpful'
what: The Cloyne Report, published 13 July 2011, examined the diocese's handling of allegations against 19 clerics from 1996 to February 2009, after the Irish church had adopted reporting procedures. Nine complaints that should have been reported to the Gardaí were not, and none were reported to the health authorities. Bishop John Magee was found to have shown little interest in applying the guidelines for 12 years. The report said the Vatican's response to the Irish procedures allowed bishops to ignore them.

title: Ryan Commission — industrial schools run by religious orders
who: Christian Brothers (most boys' institutions), Sisters of Mercy (most girls' institutions) and other Catholic orders
cover_up: Christian Brothers sued the commission in 2004 to keep members' names out; no real names of perpetrators published; findings not to be used for prosecutions; state Department of Education inspections failed
what: The Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse reported on 20 May 2009 after a nine-year investigation of more than 250 church-run institutions that held over 30,000 children from the 1930s to the 1990s. It found sexual abuse 'endemic' in boys' institutions run mainly by the Christian Brothers; the Sisters of Mercy ran most girls' institutions. The 2,600-page report names no perpetrators after a Christian Brothers lawsuit. A parallel state redress scheme paid about 12,000 people an average of €65,000.

title: Scoping Inquiry — abuse in religious-run schools
who: 42 religious orders that ran day and boarding schools
what: The state Scoping Inquiry, published 3 September 2024, recorded 2,395 allegations of sexual abuse against 884 alleged abusers at 308 schools run by 42 religious orders, mostly from the 1960s to the 1990s. 590 allegations involving 190 alleged abusers concerned 17 special schools. More than half of the alleged abusers are dead. The government announced a full Commission of Investigation.

title: Archdiocese of Boston — Spotlight 2002 and Massachusetts AG report 2003
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Boston; Cardinal Bernard Law
cover_up: Accused priests reassigned with Cardinal Law's personal involvement; church alerted law enforcement only twice in six decades; bishops sought leniency for priests and withheld information from prosecutors
what: After the Boston Globe Spotlight series beginning January 2002, Cardinal Law resigned in December 2002. The Massachusetts Attorney General's report of 23 July 2003 found at least 237 priests and 13 other church workers accused of abusing at least 789 minors over six decades, and 'overwhelming evidence' that Law knew and took part in reassigning abusers. No criminal statute allowed charging church leaders.

title: Pennsylvania grand jury — six dioceses
who: Six Pennsylvania Catholic dioceses
cover_up: Abusers moved and protected, some later promoted; reports brushed aside; most crimes beyond statute of limitations
what: A 23-member statewide grand jury report released by Attorney General Josh Shapiro on 14 August 2018 identified 301 'predator priests' and at least 1,000 child victims over about 70 years in six dioceses. The roughly 1,400-page report found bishops 'went to great lengths to keep it secret' and moved abusers. Most crimes were too old to prosecute.

title: Illinois Attorney General — clergy abuse report
who: Six Catholic dioceses of Illinois
cover_up: Before the investigation the dioceses had publicly listed only 103 substantiated abusers
what: Attorney General Kwame Raoul's report of 23 May 2023, from an investigation opened in 2018, named 451 Catholic clerics and religious brothers who abused at least 1,997 children in Illinois' six dioceses over decades. Before the inquiry the dioceses had publicly listed 103 substantiated abusers.

title: John Jay College study — US Catholic clergy 1950–2002
who: US Conference of Catholic Bishops (commissioned study)
cover_up: Of accused priests whose cases reached police, only one in three was charged; 3% served prison time
what: The John Jay College of Criminal Justice study, commissioned by the US bishops and released 27 February 2004, counted 4,392 priests and deacons (about 4% of clergy) accused of abusing 10,667 minors between 1950 and 2002. Reported abuse peaked in the 1970s; one-third of allegations were made only in 2002–03. 149 priests with more than 10 allegations each accounted for 27% of allegations. Costs to the church were put at $472 million at the time.

title: Maryland Attorney General — Archdiocese of Baltimore
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Baltimore
cover_up: Archdiocese often failed to report to authorities or remove abusers; some accused allowed to retire with support; post-2002 public list omitted known abusers
what: The Maryland Attorney General's report, released in redacted form on 5 April 2023, identified 156 priests and others associated with the Archdiocese of Baltimore who abused more than 600 children over 80 years. Attorney General Anthony Brown described 'repeated coverup' by the church. A judge ordered the names and titles of 37 people redacted.

title: Missouri Attorney General — four Catholic dioceses
who: Archdiocese of St. Louis and dioceses of Kansas City–St. Joseph, Jefferson City, Springfield–Cape Girardeau
what: Attorney General Eric Schmitt reported on 13 September 2019 on a review, opened in August 2018, of records of more than 2,000 priests who served in Missouri since 1945. It found 163 credible allegations of abuse or misconduct against minors by diocesan priests and deacons; 83 of the accused had died and the statute of limitations had expired for 46 alleged crimes. Twelve former priests were referred for prosecution.

title: Michigan Attorney General — clergy abuse investigation
who: Catholic dioceses of Michigan
what: Attorney General Dana Nessel said on 23 December 2019 that the state investigation had identified 270 priests alleged to have abused 552 victims. Seven priests had been charged in 2019, two of whom had pleaded guilty. Most cases could not be prosecuted because of statutes of limitations.

title: Archdiocese of Agaña — Archbishop Apuron and bankruptcy
who: Archdiocese of Agaña; former Archbishop Anthony Apuron
what: A Vatican tribunal of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith found former Archbishop Anthony Apuron guilty of some charges including sexual abuse of minors in March 2018; the appeal was rejected in February 2019. He was barred from office and from living in Guam but not laicised; he denies the allegations. The archdiocese filed for bankruptcy in January 2019 facing more than 200 lawsuits naming 35 clergy, teachers and scoutmasters. Guam lifted the civil statute of limitations in 2016.

title: Winter Commission — Archdiocese of St. John's
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of St. John's; Archbishop Alphonsus Penney
cover_up: Report assigned Archbishop Penney part of the blame for covering up abuse
what: Archbishop Alphonsus Penney commissioned former Lieutenant Governor Gordon Winter in May 1989 to inquire into sexual abuse of children by clergy of the archdiocese. The 1990 report assigned Penney part of the blame for covering up abuse, and he resigned after its release.

title: Royal Commission — Catholic Church data, Australia
who: Catholic Church in Australia, incl. St John of God Brothers (40.4% of brothers accused)
what: Data presented to the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse on 6 February 2017 showed 4,444 people reported abuse to Catholic authorities between 1980 and 2015, at more than 1,000 institutions, naming 1,880 alleged perpetrators. About 7% of priests who served between 1950 and 2010 were alleged perpetrators; 40.4% of St John of God Brothers were accused. Religious brothers (32%) and priests (30%) were the largest groups. The commission referred 309 cases to police.

title: Diocese of Ballarat — Gerald Ridsdale and Royal Commission Case Study 28
who: Catholic Diocese of Ballarat; Bishop Ronald Mulkearns
cover_up: Ridsdale moved through about 13 postings 1962–1991; Mulkearns knew by late 1975; a senior police officer in 1972 offered a detective promotion to stop investigating Monsignor John Day
what: Gerald Ridsdale, ordained 1961, was convicted in a series of trials from 1993 of abusing more than 70 children; he died in prison in 2025. He was moved between parishes including Mildura, Swan Hill, Warrnambool, Apollo Bay, Edenhope and Mortlake, then to Sydney. The Royal Commission's Ballarat report of 6 December 2017 found Bishop Mulkearns knew of his offending by late 1975 and still reappointed him, a 'catastrophic' failure. It also found police obstruction of a 1972 investigation of Monsignor John Day.

title: Cardinal George Pell — convicted 2018, acquitted 2020
who: Cardinal George Pell (former Archbishop of Melbourne, Vatican treasurer)
what: A Melbourne jury convicted Cardinal George Pell in December 2018 on five charges relating to two choirboys at St Patrick's Cathedral in 1996. On 7 April 2020 the High Court of Australia unanimously quashed the convictions and entered acquittals; he had served more than 400 days in prison. Separately, Royal Commission findings released in May 2020 said Pell was aware of abuse by clergy in the 1970s; he disputed this. He died in 2023.

title: Royal Commission into Abuse in Care — Catholic institutions
who: Catholic Church in Aotearoa New Zealand; St John of God Brothers at Marylands School
cover_up: Church relied on psychiatrists' opinions to transfer abusers to other ministries where they reoffended; commission recommended investigating priests transferred to Papua New Guinea
what: The Royal Commission's final report, Whanaketia, published 24 July 2024, found about 200,000 people were abused in state and faith-based care from 1950 to 2019. It found Catholic responses inadequate, noting a 2020 church briefing that 14% of clergy were accused over 1950–1999, and singled out Marylands School in Christchurch for some of the highest levels of sexual abuse. It found abusers were transferred to other ministries and recommended an inquiry into priests sent to Papua New Guinea.

title: IICSA — Roman Catholic Church in England and Wales
who: Catholic Church in England and Wales; Cardinal Vincent Nichols
cover_up: Accused priests reassigned to other parishes; Holy See and Apostolic Nuncio refused to provide a witness statement
what: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse reported on 10 November 2020 that the Church in England and Wales received more than 900 complaints involving over 3,000 instances of child sexual abuse between 1970 and 2015, with more than 100 allegations a year since 2016. It found the church put its reputation before children and criticised Cardinal Nichols. The Holy See declined to provide a witness statement.

title: IICSA — Ampleforth and Downside Benedictine schools
who: English Benedictine Congregation — Ampleforth Abbey and Downside Abbey schools
cover_up: Both institutions for decades avoided giving police and social services information; 'tell them nothing' approach after 2001
what: The IICSA report of 9 August 2018 found a culture of acceptance of abuse at Ampleforth and Downside, where children as young as seven and eleven were abused over about four decades. Ten people linked to the schools, mostly monks, were convicted or cautioned for sexual or indecent-image offences. Both abbeys tried for decades to avoid passing information to police and social services.

title: IICSA — Archdiocese of Birmingham
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Birmingham
cover_up: Fr James Robinson moved parish after 1980s complaints, police not told; he fled to the US in 1985 and received archdiocesan payments for seven years; the Vicar General helped Fr Samuel Penney avoid arrest and leave the UK
what: The IICSA case study report of 20 June 2019 found more than 130 allegations against 78 people associated with the archdiocese since the 1930s. It examined priests James Robinson, Samuel Penney and John Tolkien. Robinson was moved to another parish after complaints in the 1980s without police being told, then fled to the US in 1985 while still receiving archdiocesan support; he was later extradited and jailed for 21 years.

title: Deetman Commission — Catholic Church in the Netherlands
who: Catholic dioceses and religious orders in the Netherlands
cover_up: Policy of 'not hanging out the dirty washing'; bishops and officials knew and did not act
what: The commission led by former minister Wim Deetman, set up by the church in March 2010, reported on 16 December 2011. It identified at least 800 priests, monks and other religious who abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, and estimated tens of thousands of victims. It found bishops and officials knew of the abuse and followed a policy of avoiding scandal.

title: Adriaenssens commission and Vangheluwe resignation, Belgium
who: Catholic Church in Belgium, about 29 religious orders; Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges
cover_up: Judicial raid in June 2010 seized the commission's files (later ruled disproportionate); commission members resigned
what: Bishop Roger Vangheluwe of Bruges resigned in April 2010 after admitting he abused his nephew from 1973 to 1986. The church-backed commission led by psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens received 475 complaints in six months; its report of 10 September 2010 recorded 13 suicides linked to clerical abuse and 102 verified alleged abusers in about 29 orders. In June 2010 police raided church premises and seized the commission's files (Operation Chalice/Kelk); an appeals court later ruled the raids disproportionate.

title: MHG study — German Bishops' Conference
who: German Catholic dioceses
cover_up: Researchers found personnel files had been destroyed or manipulated
what: The study by researchers from Mannheim, Heidelberg and Giessen, commissioned by the German Bishops' Conference and presented on 25 September 2018, found 1,670 clerics (4.4% of clergy) accused of abusing 3,677 minors between 1946 and 2014. The authors called the figures conservative and found that personnel files had been destroyed or manipulated.

title: Munich and Freising abuse report (Westpfahl Spilker Wastl)
who: Archdiocese of Munich and Freising; former archbishops incl. Joseph Ratzinger, Friedrich Wetter, Reinhard Marx
cover_up: Report found misconduct by archdiocesan leaders, including Joseph Ratzinger in four cases; only 4 of 173 accused priests were dismissed from the clerical state
what: The report commissioned by the archdiocese from law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, published 20 January 2022, covered 1945–2019 and found at least 497 victims and 261 possible perpetrators and accomplices, 173 of them priests. It found misconduct by Joseph Ratzinger (Archbishop 1977–1982, later Pope Benedict XVI) in four cases, Cardinal Friedrich Wetter in 21 and Cardinal Reinhard Marx in two (the full report lists three). Ratzinger corrected his statement that he had not attended a January 1980 meeting about priest Peter Hullermann, who was admitted to Munich in 1980 and later reoffended.

title: Peter Hullermann — transferred from Essen to Munich 1980
who: Archdiocese of Munich and Freising; Diocese of Essen
cover_up: Accused priest accepted into Munich for therapy in January 1980 with Cardinal Ratzinger's approval, then reassigned to pastoral work where he abused again; remained a priest until 2010
what: In January 1980 the Munich archdiocese under Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger agreed to receive Fr Peter Hullermann from the Diocese of Essen for therapy after he had been suspended there over abuse of a boy. He was then given pastoral work, abused minors again, and in June 1986 was convicted, fined 4,000 marks and given an 18-month suspended sentence with five years' probation. He kept serving in Bavarian parishes until the archdiocese suspended him in March 2010. Then vicar general Gerhard Gruber took 'full responsibility' for letting him back into pastoral work.

title: Regensburger Domspatzen choir — Weber report
who: Regensburger Domspatzen cathedral choir and boarding schools, Diocese of Regensburg
cover_up: Report faulted choir director Georg Ratzinger for 'looking away' and said former bishop Gerhard Ludwig Müller bore 'clear responsibility' for weaknesses in investigating
what: Lawyer Ulrich Weber's final report of 18 July 2017 found that 547 boys at the cathedral choir's schools were, 'with a high degree of plausibility', victims of physical or sexual abuse or both between 1945 and 1992: about 500 cases of physical violence and 67 of sexual violence, by 49 people in all. Violence was worst at the choir's preparatory school. The report faulted Georg Ratzinger, choir director 1964–1994, for 'looking away' and failing to intervene; he said he knew of physical abuse but not sexual abuse.

title: Canisius-Kolleg Berlin and Jesuit schools
who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits), Canisius-Kolleg Berlin and St. Blasien
cover_up: Superiors helped one admitted abuser, Fr Wolfgang S., emigrate to South America; offences time-barred
what: In January 2010 Fr Klaus Mertes, rector of the Jesuit Canisius-Kolleg in Berlin, wrote to about 600 former pupils who attended between 1975 and 1989, apologising for 'systematic assaults' by two priests who had taught there and asking other victims to come forward; he said there had been 'a culture of looking away'. The revelations opened the German church abuse scandal. Legal action was unlikely because of time limits. One of the former teachers, Wolfgang S., then living in South America, admitted he had abused children and young people for years and said he had told his Jesuit superiors in 1991.

title: Cardinal Groër affair and Klasnic victims' commission, Austria
who: Archdiocese of Vienna; Austrian Bishops' Conference; Independent Victims' Protection Commission (Klasnic Commission)
what: Archbishop of Vienna Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër stepped down in September 1995 after a former pupil, followed by others, accused him of sexual abuse; in 1998 Austrian bishops said they considered the allegations well founded, and the Holy See opened an inquiry. In spring 2010 the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission chaired by Waltraud Klasnic. By 31 August 2021, according to the church's victims' foundation, payments had been approved in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total. At Kremsmünster Abbey, the former head of the boarding school was jailed for 12 years in 2013 for crimes against 24 former pupils, 15 of them victims of sexual abuse.

title: CIASE (Sauvé Commission) — Catholic Church in France
who: Catholic Church in France (commissioned by bishops and religious orders)
cover_up: Commission called the abuse 'massive' and 'systemic' and said the church must accept institutional responsibility
what: The Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church, chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé, reported on 5 October 2021. Using a population survey, it estimated about 216,000 people were abused as minors by clergy and religious from 1950 to 2020, and about 330,000 including lay people working in church institutions. Archive research put the number of abusive clergy and religious at 2,900 to 3,200, a floor of 2.5% to 2.8% of the roughly 115,000 who served, and it described the abuse as massive and its causes as systemic.

title: Bernard Preynat and Cardinal Barbarin, Lyon
who: Archdiocese of Lyon; Fr Bernard Preynat; Cardinal Philippe Barbarin
cover_up: Cardinal Barbarin convicted in March 2019 of failing to report abuse (suspended six months), cleared on appeal and by France's highest court in April 2021
what: Fr Bernard Preynat was accused of abusing about 80 Boy Scouts between 1971 and 1991; many cases were time-barred and he was tried for assaults on 10 minors from 1986 to 1991. A church tribunal found him guilty and removed him from the priesthood (announced 4 July 2019), and on 16 March 2020 a Lyon court sentenced him to five years in prison. Cardinal Philippe Barbarin was convicted in March 2019 of not reporting him and given a six-month suspended sentence; an appeal court acquitted him in January 2020 and the Cour de cassation upheld that in April 2021. Pope Francis accepted his resignation on 6 March 2020.

title: Spanish Ombudsman report on Church abuse
who: Catholic Church in Spain
what: Spain's first official inquiry into clergy abuse, a nearly 800-page report by Ombudsman Ángel Gabilondo presented to parliament on 27 October 2023 after an 18-month investigation of 487 cases, criticised the church's response as often minimising or denying the problem. A GAD3 survey of 8,000 adults in the report found 1.13% said they had been abused as children by clergy or lay church members and 0.6% by clergy. Gabilondo did not extrapolate a victim count; media applying the percentages to Spain's adult population put the figure at about 440,000 (or about 200,000 for clergy alone). The Spanish bishops apologised but disputed the media figures.

title: University of Zurich pilot study — Catholic Church in Switzerland
who: Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders (commissioned study)
what: Historians at the University of Zurich, led by Monika Dommann and Marietta Meier and commissioned by the Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders, published a pilot study in September 2023 on sexual abuse in the Swiss Catholic Church since the mid-20th century. They documented 1,002 cases involving 510 accused people and 921 victims; 74% of the documents concerned abuse of minors. More than half the cases occurred in pastoral work and about 30% in Catholic children's homes, schools and boarding schools. The researchers called the cases 'the tip of the iceberg' and found that church criminal law was hardly ever applied, with many cases kept secret, covered up or trivialised.

title: Independent Commission — Catholic Church in Portugal
who: Catholic Church in Portugal (commission set up by the bishops)
what: An independent commission set up by the Portuguese church and led by child psychiatrist Pedro Strecht reported on 13 February 2023, after hearing from more than 500 survivors, that at least 4,815 children had been abused in the church since 1950. Most offences were time-barred; 25 cases were passed to prosecutors.

title: Poland — bishops' 2019 figures, Sekielski films and sanctions on bishops
who: Polish Episcopal Conference; Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź; Bishop Edward Janiak; Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz
cover_up: Bishops sanctioned by the Vatican for protecting abusers: Janiak (Kalisz) ordered to resign June 2020; Głódź (Gdańsk) removed August 2020 after covering up abuse by Henryk Jankowski and Franciszek Cybula
what: In March 2019 the Polish Episcopal Conference released a study reporting 382 priests accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. The Sekielski brothers' documentaries 'Tell No One' (May 2019, over 23 million YouTube views) and 'Hide and Seek' (May 2020) led to Vatican investigations of bishops under Vos estis lux mundi. In June 2020 Pope Francis put the Diocese of Kalisz under an apostolic administrator and on 17 October 2020 accepted the resignation of Bishop Edward Janiak, accused in 'Hide and Seek' of failing to act against an accused priest. Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź was also investigated, and on 6 November 2020 the Vatican imposed disciplinary measures on Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz, who died ten days later.

title: Antonio Provolo Institute for the Deaf, Verona
who: Compagnia di Maria per l'educazione dei sordomuti (Provolo Institute); Diocese of Verona
cover_up: Fr Nicola Corradi, accused in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese in 2011, was working at the institute's branch in Argentina, where he went on to abuse children
what: In 2009 former students of the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona went public: 67 people said they had been abused by 24 priests, lay people and religious brothers, and named Fr Nicola Corradi as being in Argentina. In 2012 the Diocese of Verona asked victims for forgiveness and sanctioned accused members, but Corradi was not among them and was never charged in Italy. He kept working at the Provolo school in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016 and convicted in 2019.

title: Próvolo Institute, Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza) — convictions 2019
who: Provolo Institute for the Deaf (Argentina branch); Fr Nicola Corradi, Fr Horacio Corbacho, gardener Armando Gómez; Sr Kumiko Kosaka charged
cover_up: Corradi had been accused in Verona in 2009 yet continued at the Argentine school; Japanese nun Kumiko Kosaka charged with abuse and covering up
what: Priests Nicola Corradi (Italian) and Horacio Corbacho and other staff of the Provolo school for deaf children in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza were arrested in 2016, charged with abusing at least two dozen students. On 25 November 2019 a Mendoza court convicted Corradi, Corbacho and gardener Armando Gómez of abusing children at the school between 2004 and 2016; the victims in the trial were 10 former students. Corradi was sentenced to 42 years, Corbacho to 45 and Gómez to 18. Nun Kumiko Kosaka was charged in 2017 with helping the abuse and with physically abusing students.

title: Fr Julio César Grassi — Happy Children Foundation
who: Fr Julio César Grassi, Fundación Felices los Niños
what: Fr Julio César Grassi, who ran the Fundación Felices los Niños for poor children, was convicted in 2009 by Oral Criminal Court 1 of Morón of aggravated sexual abuse (two counts) and aggravated corruption of a minor in his care, and sentenced to 15 years. The conviction was upheld by the provincial courts, and on 21 March 2017 Argentina's Supreme Court rejected his final appeal, making the sentence definitive; he was by then in prison in Campana.

title: Fr Alfonso Pedrajas diary — Jesuits in Bolivia
who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits) in Bolivia
cover_up: Confessed to his instructor in 1978, who covered it up; El País reported seven provincial superiors and about ten Bolivian and Spanish clerics covered for him
what: Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas (1943–2009) was made deputy director of the Juan XXIII boarding school in Cochabamba, Bolivia in October 1971 and became its director about three years later. His diary, published by El País on 30 April 2023, admits he abused dozens of children while teaching at schools in Latin America, mainly in Cochabamba, and estimates the number at about 85. In 1978 in Spain he spoke about the abuse to his Jesuit instructor; no process was opened and he was not removed. El País reported that at least seven provincial superiors and about ten Bolivian and Spanish clerics covered up his crimes. He died in Cochabamba in September 2009 and was never prosecuted.

title: Fernando Karadima, Bishop Barros and Chile's bishops' resignation offer
who: Archdiocese of Santiago; Fr Fernando Karadima; Bishop Juan Barros; Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati
cover_up: Parishioners reported Karadima to Archbishop Fresno in 1984; Cardinal Errázuriz shelved a credible 2004–05 investigation; Barros, a Karadima protégé, made bishop of Osorno in 2015
what: The Vatican found Fr Fernando Karadima guilty of sexual abuse in 2011 and sentenced him to a life of prayer and penance; Pope Francis dismissed him from the priesthood on 27 September 2018, announced the next day. Four of his protégés became bishops, including Juan Barros of Osorno, whom Francis had defended. After receiving a 2,300-page report from Archbishop Charles Scicluna, Francis wrote in April 2018 that he had been mistaken in his assessment of the situation in Chile. Every bishop in Chile offered to resign in May 2018; by the end of June five resignations, including Barros's (11 June), had been accepted. In October 2018 an appeals court found the Archdiocese of Santiago liable for covering up for Karadima in a suit by three survivors naming Cardinals Errázuriz and Ezzati.

title: Marist Brothers Chile — Brother Abel Pérez
who: Marist Brothers in Chile
cover_up: After confessing to superiors in 2010, Pérez was transferred to Peru
what: In 2017 the Chilean Marist Brothers acknowledged that Brother Abel Pérez abused at least 14 minors between the 1970s and 2000. He had confessed to superiors in 2010 and was then transferred to Peru. Police investigated complaints at many of the order's schools.

title: Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana — suppressed by the Vatican 2025
who: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae; founder Luis Fernando Figari
network: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana)
cover_up: Abuse reported by journalists in 2015 after years of internal silence; journalists faced legal action; Vatican commission in 2023 led to mass expulsions
what: Journalists Pedro Salinas and Paola Ugaz exposed abuse by founder Luis Fernando Figari and associates in the 2015 book 'Mitad monjes, mitad soldados'. An apostolic visitor was appointed in 2015. In February 2017 the group gave Peruvian prosecutors information from an expert report on sexual abuse of minors by Figari and four former members, and the Vatican barred Figari from contact with members. After an investigation by Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Mgr Jordi Bertomeu, the Vatican expelled Figari in August 2024 over physical, psychological and sexual violence, including against minors. The society was formally suppressed by a decree signed on 14 April 2025.

title: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried
what: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.

title: Mexican bishops' conference — 426 priests investigated
who: Conferencia del Episcopado Mexicano
cover_up: El Universal reported only six convictions out of 156 alleged abuse cases involving minors, 2009–2019
what: On 14 January 2020 the Mexican Episcopal Conference said it was investigating 426 priests over the previous ten years: 271 cases of abuse of minors in church settings and 155 other proceedings. It said 217 priests had been removed from their duties. El Universal reported in February 2020 that prosecutors had opened 156 investigations into such sexual offences by religious figures from 2009 to 2019, but four prosecutors' offices recorded only six sentences.

title: Venezuela — priests accused or convicted 2001–2022
who: Catholic Church in Venezuela
cover_up: Three of the priests served little or no sentence and returned to ministry
what: A 2022 Washington Post investigation found at least 10 Catholic priests accused or convicted of sexual abuse in Venezuela between 2001 and 2022, with complaints in at least eleven states. Three served little or no sentence and returned to the priesthood. The church confirmed the report's accuracy and announced an investigation.

title: Brazil — priest convictions
who: Catholic dioceses in Brazil
what: In 2005 Fr Tarcísio Tadeu Spricigo and Fr Geraldo da Consolação Machado were convicted of child molestation in Brazil. Fr Felix Barbosa Carreiro was arrested and charged in Maranhão after police found him in a hotel room with four teenage boys. No national inquiry has been held in Brazil, the country with the world's largest Catholic population.

title: Crimen sollicitationis — secrecy instruction (1962)
who: Holy See — Holy Office (now Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith)
cover_up: Church proceedings to be kept absolutely confidential under automatic excommunication, binding tribunal members, accusers and witnesses
what: The Holy Office instruction Crimen sollicitationis, approved by Pope John XXIII on 16 March 1962 and restating a 1922 instruction, governed canonical cases of solicitation in confession and also obscene acts with pre-adolescent children. It required absolute secrecy under pain of automatic excommunication. Many bishops did not know it was in their archives until press reports in 2003. Canon lawyer Thomas Doyle called the secrecy rules 'an explicit written policy to cover up cases', while others argue it did not bar reporting to police. It stayed in force until 2001.

title: Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela / De delictis gravioribus (2001)
who: Holy See — Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, prefect)
cover_up: All abuse-of-minor cases reserved to the CDF under pontifical secret
what: Pope John Paul II's motu proprio Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela (30 April 2001), with the CDF letter De delictis gravioribus of 18 May 2001 signed by its prefect Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, reserved to the CDF the delict of a cleric's sexual offence with a minor under 18, required bishops to notify the CDF after a preliminary investigation, and stated that such cases were subject to the pontifical secret, which remained until December 2019. In May 2014 the Holy See told the UN Committee against Torture that from 2004 to 2013 the CDF had studied 3,420 credible cases of abuse of minors and that 884 priests had been dismissed from the clerical state.

title: Benedict XVI Pastoral Letter to the Catholics of Ireland (2010)
who: Pope Benedict XVI
what: On 19 March 2010, after the Ryan and Murphy reports, Pope Benedict XVI issued a pastoral letter to the Catholics of Ireland. Addressing abuse victims and their families, he wrote: 'You have suffered grievously and I am truly sorry. I know that nothing can undo the wrong you have endured.' Critics said it did not address systemic failures.

title: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child — Holy See review (2014)
who: Holy See
cover_up: Committee found abusive clergy were reassigned without police notification, bishops not required to report to civil authorities, and a code of silence
what: On 5 February 2014 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child said it was gravely concerned that the Holy See had not acknowledged the extent of the crimes, had not taken the necessary measures against child sexual abuse, and had adopted policies that allowed abuse to continue. It said the Holy See had consistently placed the church's reputation and the protection of perpetrators above children's best interests, accused it of transferring abusive priests to new parishes, urged it to require clergy to report abuse to police, and criticised a 'code of silence' under which whistleblowers were ostracised, demoted and fired.

title: Pope Francis' letter to Chile's bishops and the Scicluna mission (2018)
who: Pope Francis; Archbishop Charles Scicluna; Mgr Jordi Bertomeu
what: After defending Bishop Juan Barros in January 2018, Pope Francis sent Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Mgr Jordi Bertomeu, who took 64 depositions in New York and Santiago; their report ran to more than 2,300 pages. In a letter of 8 April 2018 Francis wrote that he had 'made serious errors in the assessment and perception of the situation, in particular through the lack of reliable and balanced information', and summoned the Chilean bishops to Rome, where all of them offered to resign in May 2018.

title: Vos estis lux mundi (2019) and February 2019 summit
who: Pope Francis
what: Three months after a February 2019 Vatican summit of bishops' conference presidents on abuse, Pope Francis issued Vos estis lux mundi, published on 9 May 2019. It requires clerics and religious to report suspected abuse and cover-ups promptly to church authorities, requires every diocese to set up a public reporting system, and lets bishops be investigated for abuse or cover-up. It applies 'without prejudice' to state reporting laws but does not itself require reporting to civil authorities. A revised permanent version was decreed on 25 March 2023 and took effect on 30 April 2023.

title: Pontifical secret lifted for abuse cases (December 2019)
who: Pope Francis
what: On 17 December 2019 Pope Francis issued the instruction 'On the confidentiality of legal proceedings', removing the pontifical secret from cases of sexual abuse of minors and vulnerable persons, child abuse material and concealment of such crimes. Information must still be treated with 'security, integrity and confidentiality' but can be made available to state authorities, and church officials were told to comply with civil laws. In a separate change the same day, the age limit in the Vatican's definition of child abuse material was raised from 14 to 18.

title: McCarrick Report (Holy See, November 2020)
who: Holy See; former Cardinal Theodore McCarrick
cover_up: A 1999 warning letter reached Pope John Paul II; an inquiry stalled after three of four US bishops gave 'inaccurate and incomplete information'; McCarrick was promoted to Washington in 2000
what: The Holy See's report of 10 November 2020 found that Pope John Paul II appointed Theodore McCarrick Archbishop of Washington in 2000 despite a letter from Cardinal John O'Connor dated 28 October 1999 warning that the appointment would risk serious scandal, and after McCarrick denied the allegations. Benedict XVI did not order an investigation but had McCarrick told to retire in 2006 and keep a lower profile, which he did not do. The report said Francis did not learn that McCarrick was accused of abusing a minor until 2017. On 11 January 2019 the CDF found him guilty of solicitation in confession and sexual offences with minors and adults, and he was dismissed from the priesthood (announced 16 February 2019). A Massachusetts charge of assaulting a 16-year-old at a 1974 wedding reception was dismissed on 30 August 2023 after he was found incompetent to stand trial because of dementia. He d

title: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
cover_up: Wesołowski recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic
what: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, and Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013. A church tribunal found him guilty and the Vatican announced his laicisation on 27 June 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor indicted him for abusing children in the Dominican Republic in 2008–2013 and for possessing child abuse images, but he was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, was arrested in Poland in February 2014; on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic (2009–2013) and two in Poland.

title: Vatican tribunal — diplomat Carlo Capella and the Martinelli trial
who: Holy See diplomat Mgr Carlo Capella; St Pius X pre-seminary
what: On 23 June 2018 the Vatican tribunal convicted Mgr Carlo Capella, recalled in 2017 from the Holy See's embassy in Washington, of possessing and sharing child abuse images and sentenced him to five years. In October 2020 the first Vatican criminal trial for sexual abuse began: Fr Gabriele Martinelli was accused of abusing an altar boy at the St Pius X pre-seminary inside the Vatican, and former rector Enrico Radice was charged with aiding and abetting.

title: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
cover_up: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994
what: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused children for decades from the 1950s in Northern Ireland, the Republic and the United States; the BBC put the number at at least 143. In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, attended church meetings where two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy; their evidence was never given to police. The Irish government's delay in acting on the RUC's extradition request led to the collapse of the Reynolds coalition in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland in 1994 for abusing dozens of children there, and in July 1997 was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children in the Republic. He died in the Curragh Prison in August 1997. The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (2017) found the Norbertine order moved him to another diocese despite knowing his history.

title: Diocese of Raphoe — Fr Eugene Greene
who: Catholic Diocese of Raphoe
what: Fr Eugene Greene, the most notorious offender in the Diocese of Raphoe, was sentenced in 1999 to 12 years in prison for abusing 26 boys over 20 years. A church safeguarding review published on 30 November 2011 found allegations against 14 Raphoe priests between 1975 and 2010, four of whom had been convicted, and pointed to 'significant errors of judgement' by successive bishops. Former bishop Séamus Hegarty said his past practice was 'sometimes poor' and apologised.

title: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland — review 2020
who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (with Scout Association of Ireland), now Scouting Ireland
cover_up: Organisations shielded known or suspected abusers after abuse was reported
what: A review published in May 2020 found that over several decades before their 2004 merger into Scouting Ireland, the Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland and the Scout Association of Ireland shielded 275 known or suspected abusers. Scouting Ireland accepted the findings and apologised.

title: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Sisters of Nazareth
who: Poor Sisters of Nazareth
what: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry found in May 2019 that children in Nazareth House orphanages from 1933 to 1984 suffered sexual abuse 'of the utmost depravity'. Police received more than 300 complaints. In 2025 the Sisters agreed to pay up to £5.75 million to survivors and three former staff were convicted.

title: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Smyllum Park and Bellevue (Daughters of Charity)
who: Daughters of Charity of St Vincent de Paul
what: About 11,600 children passed through Smyllum Park orphanage, run by the Daughters of Charity from 1864 to 1981. The inquiry's October 2018 findings said children were sexually abused by priests, a trainee priest, sisters, staff and a volunteer, and beaten with implements. Seventeen people were later charged; in 2025 the order agreed to pay up to £10 million.

title: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Fort Augustus Abbey and Carlekemp (Benedictines)
who: English Benedictine Congregation — Fort Augustus Abbey School and Carlekemp Priory School
cover_up: Complaints to senior monks were inadequately handled; after one complaint the school did not tell police and sent the monk, Denis Chrysostom Alexander, back to Australia
what: On 11 August 2021 Lady Smith published the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's findings on residential care run by the Benedictine monks of Fort Augustus Abbey between 1948 and 1991, concluding that children at Carlekemp Priory School, North Berwick, and Fort Augustus Abbey School suffered sexual, physical and emotional abuse; 43 witnesses gave evidence in 2019. A 2013 BBC investigation had presented evidence against seven Fort Augustus monks. Denis Chrysostom Alexander, sent back to Australia after parents complained, was arrested in Sydney in 2017, returned to Scotland in January 2020, pleaded guilty in June 2021 to abusing two boys and was jailed for four years and five months. Robert MacKenzie was extradited from Canada in 2020 but the case was dropped in 2021.

title: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Marist and Christian Brothers schools
who: Marist Brothers (St Joseph's College Dumfries, St Columba's College Largs); Christian Brothers (St Ninian's, Falkland)
what: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's findings on the Christian Brothers, published on 17 February 2021, concluded that the regime at St Ninian's Residential Care Home, Falkland, exposed children to risks of sexual, physical and psychological danger, and that between 1953 and 1983 those risks materialised for many children; 42 witnesses gave evidence. The inquiry also examined the Marist Brothers' St Joseph's College, Dumfries and St Columba's College, Largs, with findings published later in 2021. Two Brothers were jailed in 2016 for abuse at St Ninian's.

title: Fr Paul Moore — moved by his bishop to Toronto
who: Diocese of Galloway; Bishop Maurice Taylor
cover_up: Bishop Maurice Taylor sent Moore to Toronto and Fort Augustus
what: Fr Francis 'Paul' Moore was found guilty at the High Court in Glasgow in 2018 of abusing three boys in Ayrshire in the 1970s and indecently assaulting a student priest in 1995, and was jailed for nine years. He had confessed his attraction to boys to Bishop Maurice Taylor of Galloway in 1996; Taylor sent him to a treatment centre in Toronto and to Fort Augustus Abbey, removed him from ministry but let him live in a church-bought house, and did not report him.

title: Indian Residential Schools run by Catholic entities — TRC and papal apology
who: Catholic dioceses and orders (incl. Oblates of Mary Immaculate) that ran about 44 of 80 schools at the 1931 peak (TRC says about 70% overall)
cover_up: Federal government funded and mandated attendance; Catholic entities cited lack of funds to compensate
what: More than 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children were forced to attend Canada's government-funded residential schools between the 1870s and 1997; the Catholic Church ran over half of them. In 2015 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's chair said the commissioners had concluded that 'cultural genocide' was the best description of the system. In July 2022 at Maskwacis, Alberta, Pope Francis asked forgiveness 'for the wrong done by so many Christians to the Indigenous peoples', and on his return flight described the system as genocide.

title: Basilian Fathers — Canadian convictions
who: Congregation of St. Basil (Basilian Fathers)
what: Basilian priest William Hodgson Marshall pleaded guilty in 2011 to 16 counts of indecent assault and one of sexual assault from 1952–1986 in Windsor, Toronto and Sudbury schools. Robert Whyte pleaded guilty in 1990 to abusing 18 children (1962–1982); Kenneth O'Keefe received house arrest in 2012–2013. In April 2020 the Supreme Court of Canada let stand an award of over $2.5 million, including $500,000 punitive damages, against the Basilians.

title: Fr Eric Dejaeger — Oblate in Nunavut
who: Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate; Belgian-born Fr Eric Dejaeger
what: Belgian-born Oblate missionary Eric Dejaeger had served a five-year sentence in the early 1990s for 11 counts of sexual and indecent assault against children in Baker Lake, Nunavut. When charged over Igloolik he fled to Belgium, where he lived in Oblate homes for 16 years despite an international warrant; Oblate officials acknowledged they knew he was about to leave. Returned to Canada in 2011, he was convicted on 12 September 2014 of 24 further counts, and with eight guilty pleas was sentenced in 2015 for 32 sex crimes against Inuit children in Igloolik between 1978 and 1982. He received 19 years (eight after time served); appeals were dismissed in 2018.

title: Archdiocese of Los Angeles — settlements 2007 and 2024
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Los Angeles; Cardinal Roger Mahony
cover_up: In 2013 Archbishop Gómez removed Cardinal Mahony from public duties over his handling of abusive clergy
what: In July 2007 the Archdiocese of Los Angeles agreed a $660 million settlement with more than 500 people who said they were abused by more than 220 priests, teachers and other church employees, and Cardinal Roger Mahony apologised. In October 2024 it agreed to pay $880 million to 1,353 people, which experts called the largest single child sex abuse settlement with a Catholic archdiocese; total payouts reached more than $1.5 billion. In February 2013 Archbishop José Gómez barred Mahony from public ministry over his handling of abusers.

title: Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady
who: Diocese of Stockton; Bishop Roger Mahony (later Cardinal Archbishop of Los Angeles)
cover_up: After police declined to charge him in 1984, Bishop Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor; Mahony said he was unaware of molestation reports, although a letter about earlier abuse was in O'Grady's personnel file.
what: Irish-born priest Oliver O'Grady, ordained in 1971 for the Diocese of Stockton, abused children from about 1973 and was moved between parishes. Bishop Roger Mahony knew of concerns by 1980 and moved him in 1984. O'Grady was convicted in 1993 and sentenced to 14 years; a 1998 civil jury awarded $30 million (reduced to $7 million). Paroled and deported to Ireland in 2000, he was convicted there for child abuse images in 2012 and 2020.

title: Diocese of Lafayette — Gilbert Gauthe (first national case)
who: Diocese of Lafayette; Fr Gilbert Gauthe
cover_up: Bishop assigned him as Boy Scout chaplain in 1974 despite allegations; sent for therapy in 1976 and returned
what: Fr Gilbert Gauthe admitted abusing 37 children while serving in the Diocese of Lafayette from 1972 to 1983. In 1974 the bishop made him a Boy Scout chaplain despite allegations about altar boys. In October 1985 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 20 years; the diocese paid more than $20 million. His 1984–85 case was the first widely publicised clergy abuse prosecution in the US.

title: US diocesan bankruptcies and settlements
who: US Catholic dioceses (Portland, Tucson, Spokane, San Diego, Davenport, Milwaukee, Albany and others)
cover_up: Milwaukee: Cardinal Timothy Dolan, with Vatican approval, moved $57 million into a cemetery trust, which kept it from victims; released files showed priests moved without telling police
what: Starting with Portland in 2004, at least 13 US dioceses filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy by 2023 under abuse claims. US dioceses have paid about $4 billion to roughly 17,000 victims since the 1980s. In Milwaukee, which filed in 2011 after paying $29 million on about 200 cases, released documents showed abusive priests were moved between assignments without notifying law enforcement.

title: Christian Brothers in Australia — Ballarat and WA orphanages
who: Congregation of Christian Brothers
cover_up: Convicted Brothers Dowlan and Best were moved from junior to senior campus and continued offending; leaders knew of abuse at WA orphanages for decades
what: Data presented to the Royal Commission in February 2017 showed that 22% of Christian Brothers in Australia between 1950 and 2010 had been the subject of child sexual abuse allegations. The order made the most compensation payments of any Catholic authority: 763, totalling A$48.5 million. In Ballarat, former Brothers Edward Dowlan and Robert Best, the principal of St Alipius school, were jailed for sexual crimes against pupils.

title: Maitland-Newcastle diocese — Fletcher, Cunneen inquiry and Archbishop Wilson (acquitted)
who: Diocese of Maitland-Newcastle; Archbishop Philip Wilson
cover_up: Monsignor Cotter's letter about Fr Denis McAlinden said 'we do not think it can be real serious'
what: A NSW Special Commission of Inquiry led by Margaret Cunneen SC, triggered by Detective Chief Inspector Peter Fox's public allegations in November 2012, reported on 30 May 2014. It found no evidence that senior police obstructed investigations, but found senior diocesan officials knew of complaints against Fr Denis McAlinden from 1954 and took over 40 years to tell police. On 22 May 2018 Newcastle Local Court found Archbishop of Adelaide Philip Wilson guilty of concealing abuse by Fr James Fletcher that a victim had told him about in 1976; on 6 December 2018 Judge Roy Ellis upheld his appeal, finding reasonable doubt, and quashed the conviction.

title: Marist Brothers in Australia
who: Marist Brothers
cover_up: Royal Commission found the order failed to act on complaints against a Brother at Marist College Ashgrove; a Brother pleaded guilty in 2020 to concealing abuse
what: Data presented to the Royal Commission in February 2017 showed that 20% of Marist Brothers in Australia between 1950 and 2010 had been the subject of child sexual abuse allegations. Brother William Wade, a former headmaster at Marist schools in Canberra, Hamilton (Newcastle) and Kogarah, was jailed for 18 months in 2017 for abusing two boys (in 1976 and about 1980). In February 2020 he became the first senior Catholic in Australia to plead guilty to concealing child sexual abuse by colleagues, and in September 2020 was sentenced to four months, served in the community. The Marist Brothers listed 154 members accused of abusing children in June 2019.

title: Marylands School and Hebron Trust — St John of God Brothers
who: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God
network: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God
cover_up: Brother Bernard McGrath was transferred to Australia after 1977 allegations and later put in charge of Hebron Trust; victims sometimes required to sign non-disclosure agreements
what: Marylands, a Christchurch residential school for boys with learning disabilities run by the St John of God Brothers, and the order's later Hebron Trust were described by survivors to the Royal Commission as 'hell on earth'. Its August 2023 report found widespread sexual and physical abuse: more than one in five of the 537 boys who attended Marylands reported abuse between 1955 and 1984, and 21 of the 37 Brothers who served at Marylands and in Christchurch faced abuse allegations. At Hebron Trust youths were abused by Brother Bernard McGrath, who has been convicted of more than 100 offences in New Zealand and Australia.

title: Marist Brothers and priests — New Zealand convictions
who: Marist Brothers; Society of Mary
what: A 2018 Otago Daily Times report listed nine Marist Brothers convicted of crimes against boys in New Zealand, including two at Hato Paora College. Marist priest Alan Woodcock was extradited from England and convicted in 2004 of 21 offences (1978–1987). Brother Kevin Healy was convicted in 2020. The church admitted in 2022 that 14% of its diocesan clergy had been accused since 1950.

title: Fiji — transferred clergy and Julian Fox
who: Salesians; Catholic Church in Fiji
cover_up: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating; the Fiji church knew of allegations nine years before he was charged
what: Salesian priest Julian Fox was moved to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating abuse allegations; he was jailed in Australia in 2015. The Catholic Church in Fiji knew of the allegations nine years before he was charged. In July 2020 1News reported that some of about 1,300 alleged child abuse cases involving clergy in Fiji concerned clergy from Australia and New Zealand.

title: Richard Daschbach — Topu Honis shelter, Oecusse
who: Society of the Divine Word (SVD); US-born Fr Richard Daschbach
what: US-born Divine Word missionary Richard Daschbach founded the Topu Honis children's shelter in Oecusse in 1992. After a complaint to his superiors in February 2018 he admitted the abuse to them in March 2018, and the Vatican dismissed him from the priesthood on 6 November 2018; the church did not tell the public. He was arrested in April 2019 and charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing children under 14, plus child abuse material and domestic violence counts. On 21 December 2021 a court in Oecusse sentenced him to 12 years, basing the verdict on the testimony of four victims. A report by the Dili archdiocese's Justice and Peace Commission had defended him.

title: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo — Vatican sanctions
who: Salesians; Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo (Nobel Peace laureate)
cover_up: Vatican received allegations in 2019 and imposed sanctions in 2020 but did not disclose them until a magazine reported the case in 2022
what: On 28 September 2022 Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer reported that two men said Bishop Belo had abused them and other boys in Fatumaca and Dili, before and during his time as bishop. The next day the Vatican confirmed it had received allegations in 2019 and imposed disciplinary sanctions in 2020: limits on movement and ministry, no contact with minors and no contact with Timor-Leste. The sanctions were reinforced in 2021. Belo had left Timor in 2002 and worked in Maputo, Mozambique from 2004.

title: Kerala — priest convictions and Bishop Mulakkal acquittal
who: Syro-Malabar and Latin dioceses in Kerala; Bishop Franco Mulakkal of Jalandhar
what: Fr Robin Vadakkumchery of Kottiyoor, Kannur was arrested in 2017 for raping a minor girl who gave birth in February 2017; on 16 February 2019 the Thalassery POCSO court sentenced him to 20 years, which the Kerala High Court reduced to 10 years in December 2021. In May 2014 Fr Raju Kokken of Thrissur was arrested for raping a nine-year-old girl, and the archdiocese removed him. Bishop Franco Mulakkal of Jalandhar, accused by an adult nun of repeated rape between 2014 and 2016, was arrested on 21 September 2018 and acquitted of all charges in January 2022.

title: Philippines — priest arrests and removals
who: Catholic dioceses in the Philippines; a US priest assigned in Biliran
what: In 2018 an American priest assigned in the Philippines was arrested for abusing at least 10 boys in Naval, Biliran. Other cases include a priest arrested in Marikina (2017), a priest charged in Cadiz City with raping a four-year-old (2019), an arrest in Tuguegarao for abusing a 16-year-old (2022), and a Diocese of San Carlos priest arrested in March 2023 for raping a 17-year-old choir member. Pope Francis removed a Borongan priest on 10 May 2023. There has been no national inquiry in Asia's largest Catholic country.

title: Indonesia — Syahril Parlindungan Marbun, altar boys
who: Catholic parish (church volunteer Syahril Parlindungan Marbun)
what: Police reported that Syahril Parlindungan Marbun abused 20 altar boys between 2002 and 2020, and said the number could be higher.

title: St Michael's School, Soni — Rosminian priests
who: Institute of Charity (Rosminians); English priest Kit Cunningham and three others
cover_up: The order knew of Cunningham's abuse before his death in 2010; it became public only through a BBC documentary in June 2011
what: In the 1960s four Rosminian priests, including English priest Kit Cunningham, physically and sexually abused boys at St Michael's boarding school in Soni, Tanganyika (now Tanzania). The order openly acknowledged the crimes of the four priests but in 2010 refused to pay compensation; Cunningham died in December 2010. The abuse became public in the BBC documentary 'Abused: Breaking the Silence', broadcast on 21 June 2011. A group of 22 former Soni pupils pursued a compensation claim, and former pupils of Soni and the order's Grace Dieu school in Leicestershire announced they would sue.

title: Kenya — RTÉ 'Mission to Prey' and false allegation against Fr Kevin Reynolds
who: Irish missionaries in Kenya; RTÉ
what: RTÉ's May 2011 Prime Time Investigates documentary 'Mission to Prey' reported on clerical abuse by missionaries in Africa. It wrongly accused Irish priest Fr Kevin Reynolds of fathering a child with a minor in Kenya; the allegation was shown to be untrue, RTÉ apologised and paid him a substantial libel settlement, its director general called it 'one of the gravest mistakes' RTÉ had made, and the Taoiseach cited a 'grievous' drop in standards. The Broadcasting Authority of Ireland opened an investigation. Separately in 2011 a Dutch bishop was investigated over alleged abuse of a minor 18 years earlier when he was a priest in Ngong diocese, and was retired by the church.

title: Mauritius — Irish missionary abuse and priest convictions
who: Catholic Diocese of Port Louis; Irish priest at St Joseph's College
what: A survivor has said he was abused at age 11 in the late 1950s by an Irish priest at St Joseph's College, Curepipe. On 9 October 2019 the Intermediate Court sentenced Fr Joseph-Marie Moctee to three years in prison for indecent assault on a 15-year-old boy at the presbytery in Chamarel in July 2015; he appealed. In September 2016 another priest was arrested over a complaint at St Louis Cathedral, Port Louis (complainant aged 20).

title: Slovenia — Fr Franc Frantar
who: Archdiocese of Ljubljana; Fr Franc Frantar
cover_up: Avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary until an Interpol notice was issued
what: Slovenian priest Franc Frantar was detained in 2006 for abusing up to 16 minors and later sentenced (sources give three and a half and five years). He first avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary and returned to Slovenia after Interpol issued a notice.

title: Croatia — first priest convictions
who: Catholic dioceses in Croatia
cover_up: Nediljko Ivanov, whose abuse 1983–1991 was reported in 2012, was time-barred; a church court ordered only prayer, fasting and an apology and he continued to say Mass
what: In 2000 Fr Ivan Čuček was convicted of abusing 37 girls; his three-year sentence was cut to 18 months by the Supreme Court. In 2007 Fr Drago Ljubičić of Rab became the first Croatian priest to serve prison time, three years for molesting five teenage boys. Fr Nediljko Ivanov of Bibinje became the first priest convicted by a Croatian church court, but civil prosecution was time-barred.

title: Czech Republic — Fr František Merta
who: Archdiocese of Olomouc; Archbishop Jan Graubner (alleged failure to report)
cover_up: Archbishop Graubner allegedly did not report him and moved him between parishes
what: In 2000–2001 Fr František Merta was found guilty of abusing more than 20 boys and received a two-year suspended sentence. Archbishop Jan Graubner allegedly failed to report him and moved him between parishes when problems arose.

title: Norway — Bishop Georg Müller of Trondheim
who: Territorial Prelature of Trondheim; Bishop Georg Müller
what: Georg Müller, Bishop of Trondheim from 1997 to 2009, admitted in April 2010 that he had sexually abused an altar boy about 20 years earlier while a priest in the city; the church said there were no other victims. In April 2010 the church in Norway had reported 18 abuse cases; in Denmark 17 had been reported.

title: Malta — St Joseph Home convictions
who: Missionary Society of St Paul (St Joseph Home); Maltese clergy
what: By April 2010 the church in Malta had recorded 84 allegations. Fr Charles Pulis was sentenced to six years and Fr Godwin Scerri to five years for abusing boys at a church children's home; Donald Bellizzi received three years in 2020.

title: Belgium — Halsberghe commission (2000) and convictions
who: Catholic Church in Belgium
cover_up: In about half the 32 upheld cases the accused refused to appear; 31 cases were time-barred and only one reached court; in June 2010 police seized 450 internal dossiers from the Mechelen archbishop's palace
what: A church commission chaired by Godelieve Halsberghe from 2000 received over 300 complaints and upheld 32 of 33 formal ones; 31 were time-barred. Convictions included Fr Bruno Vos (nine years in 2009 for raping four minors), Robert Borremans (five years, 2008) and two Brothers jailed for ten years each in 2005 for abusing disabled people. On 24 June 2010 police raided the archbishop's palace in Mechelen, seizing 450 dossiers, and searched Cardinal Danneels' residence.

title: Italy — no national inquiry; Rete l'Abuso count
who: Catholic Church in Italy; Italian Bishops' Conference
cover_up: In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference said priests had no obligation to report suspected abuse to police
what: Italy has no official statistics or national inquiry. The victims' network Rete l'Abuso counted about 300 cases of priests and nuns before Italian courts since 2000, with 150 to 170 convictions (October 2018). In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference said its priests had no duty to report suspected abuse to police. Cases include Fr Mauro Galli (6 years 4 months, 2014) and a former Roman Rota judge who pleaded guilty to child abuse image offences in 2018.

title: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta of Orán — convicted 2022
who: Diocese of Orán; Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
cover_up: After resigning in 2017 amid complaints he was given a post at the Vatican's APSA in December 2017; suspended in January 2019
what: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta resigned from the Diocese of Orán in August 2017, citing health, after complaints from clergy, and in December 2017 Pope Francis gave him a post created for him at the Vatican's patrimony office (APSA). Clergy had complained to the nunciature in 2015–2016 about his behaviour with seminarians and explicit images on his phone. On 4 March 2022 a court in Salta sentenced him to four and a half years for continued sexual abuse of two former seminarians, aggravated by his being a minister of religion. Included as a case of a bishop moved to the Vatican, though the victims were adults.

title: Chile — Fr José Andrés Aguirre ('Cura Tato')
who: Archdiocese of Santiago
what: Former priest José Andrés Aguirre Ovalle, known as 'Cura Tato', was convicted of sexual abuse offences and sentenced to 12 years; Chile's Supreme Court confirmed the conviction and sentence in January 2005. An appeals court had made the Archdiocese of Santiago jointly liable for 100 million pesos in damages to the victims, but the Supreme Court absolved the archdiocese of payment by a 3–2 vote. Chile removed the statute of limitations for child sexual abuse on 11 July 2019 (not retroactive).

title: Denis Chrysostom Alexander — extradition from Australia
who: Benedictine monk, Fort Augustus Abbey School
cover_up: Sent back to Australia by the school after parents complained; police not informed
what: Benedictine monk Denis 'Chrysostom' Alexander abused pupils at Fort Augustus Abbey School in Scotland in the 1970s. A 2013 BBC investigation reported that after a pupil told his parents, who complained to the school, Alexander was sent back to Australia with no warning about his offending; he became a parish priest in Sydney. Scotland requested his extradition in August 2016 and he was arrested in Sydney in January 2017. After contesting extradition he was returned to Scotland in January 2020. In June 2021 at the High Court in Edinburgh he pleaded guilty to indecent behaviour against two boys aged 12 to 14 between 1973 and 1976, and on 30 July 2021 he was jailed for four years and five months.

title: Sodalicio layman arrested with a boy, Lima 2007
who: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (consecrated layman)
network: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana)
what: In 2007 Daniel Bernardo Beltrán Murguía Ward, a consecrated layman of the Sodalitium, was found in a Lima hostel photographing an 11-year-old boy; police reported photos of two other boys on his camera. He denied the charges and was removed from the group.

title: IICSA — Anglican Church investigation report
who: Church of England; Church in Wales
cover_up: Inquiry found the Church gave 'excessive attention' to alleged perpetrators over victims, ignored safeguarding advice, and used forgiveness to justify failing to respond to allegations.
what: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse published its Anglican Church investigation report on 6 October 2020. It counted 390 convicted offenders associated with the Church of England from the 1940s to 2018 and warned the true scale cannot be known. In 2018 alone, dioceses received 2,504 safeguarding concerns, 449 of them about recent child sexual abuse. It found deference to authority, clericalism and taboos about sexuality kept victims from disclosing, and that bishops kept safeguarding decision-making power.

title: Diocese of Chichester — clergy abuse (IICSA case study)
who: Church of England, Diocese of Chichester
cover_up: Clergy with known concerns (Rideout, Cotton, Graves, House) were given or kept permission to officiate; Cotton's prior conviction for indecent exposure involving a child sat in his diocesan file but was not shared with police; an archdeacon declined to report a serious indecent assault; Sussex Police dropped a 1997–98 investigation and later destroyed its records.
what: IICSA found the Diocese of Chichester had more child sexual abuse convictions than any other Church of England diocese. Roy Cotton had been ordained in the 1960s despite a prior conviction involving a child. Sussex Police investigated Cotton and Colin Pritchard in 1997–98 without charges; when Northamptonshire Police revived the case in 2006, Sussex Police had destroyed its records. The diocese's 2008–09 Past Cases Review missed the scale of abuse, and real action against abusers began only with Operation Perry in 2011.

title: Bishop Peter Ball — conviction and Church collusion
who: Church of England; 'Give a Year to God' scheme
cover_up: Lambeth Palace received seven letters supporting complainant Neil Todd's allegations in 1992 but passed only the least incriminating one to police; Archbishop George Carey wrote to the Gloucestershire Chief Constable; Ball's twin brother, also a bishop, phoned potential complainants to dissuade them; Ball accepted a caution in 1992 and was soon returned to ministry, including work in schools.
what: Peter Ball, former Bishop of Lewes and of Gloucester, ran a 'Give a Year to God' scheme for young men that the Church did not monitor. Gloucestershire police investigated in 1992 and he accepted a caution for one offence; IICSA found the Crown Prosecution Service advice to caution was wrong and other charges were possible. He pleaded guilty in 2015 and on 7 October 2015 was jailed for 32 months for offences against 18 young men over 15 years. Dame Moira Gibb's review 'An Abuse of Faith' (June 2017) found the Church colluded with Ball; Lord Carey stepped back from ministry. IICSA also noted the Duchy of Cornwall bought a property rented to Ball and his brother.

title: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa
cover_up: A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.
what: John Smyth QC, chair of the Iwerne Trust 1974–81, beat and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps and Winchester College's Christian Forum. After the 1982 Ruston Report he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, founding Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986; a 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992 and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged anywhere. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and the review found abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. Keith Makin's review was published on 7 November 2024; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.

title: Royal Commission data — Anglican Church of Australia
who: Anglican Church of Australia
