what: Data released at the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse in March 2017 showed 1,082 people lodged complaints of child sexual abuse about 1,115 incidents in the Anglican Church of Australia between 1980 and 2015. The complaints identified 569 alleged perpetrators who were clergy, teachers or volunteers, plus 133 whose church roles were unknown (702 in total).

title: Canada residential schools run by Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches
who: Anglican Church of Canada (ran over 30 schools), United Church, Presbyterian Church, with the Catholic Church and federal government
cover_up: The schools were a federal government system run by churches.
what: Canada's Indian residential schools were run for the federal government by the Anglican, Catholic, Presbyterian and United churches; the Anglican Church of Canada operated more than 30. In April 2013 Truth and Reconciliation Commission chair Justice Murray Sinclair said about 37,000 former students had filed claims for sexual abuse, serious physical abuse or other wrongful acts, and asked the public to imagine 'a school where half of the students suffered sexual and physical abuse'. The TRC's final report followed in 2015. Under the 2006 Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement, to which the Anglican, Presbyterian and United churches were parties (Anglicans ran about 30% of schools, the United Church about 10%), the Independent Assessment Process for sexual and serious physical abuse had paid C$3.18 billion to 31,103 former students by 31 March 2019 (all churches combined).

title: Southern Baptist Convention — 'Abuse of Faith' investigation
who: Southern Baptist Convention churches
what: The Houston Chronicle and San Antonio Express-News published 'Abuse of Faith' on 10–11 February 2019. They found about 380 Southern Baptist ministers and volunteers had faced allegations of sexual misconduct over the previous 20 years, with more than 700 victims. Many pleaded guilty or were convicted, more from Texas than any other state.

title: Southern Baptist Convention — Guidepost report and secret list of accused ministers
who: Southern Baptist Convention Executive Committee
cover_up: Former Executive Committee officials D. August Boto and Roger Oldham kept a private list of abusive ministers, but no one acted to keep them out of SBC pulpits; survivors met 'resistance, stonewalling, and even outright hostility' and were told church autonomy prevented action; a few senior leaders and outside counsel focused on avoiding liability.
what: Guidepost Solutions, hired after SBC delegates demanded an outside probe in 2021, released its report on 22 May 2022. It found a few senior Executive Committee leaders had for about two decades controlled the response to abuse reports to limit legal liability, ignoring or disbelieving survivors. The Executive Committee then published the previously secret list, 205 pages and 703 entries, on 26 May 2022.

title: Frank Houston — Royal Commission Case Study 18 (Assemblies of God / Hillsong)
who: Assemblies of God in Australia (now Australian Christian Churches); Hillsong Church
network: Hillsong Church / Australian Christian Churches (Assemblies of God)
cover_up: When allegations surfaced in 1999, Brian Houston, then National President of the Assemblies of God and Frank Houston's son, confronted his father, who confessed; Brian Houston and the National Executive did not refer the matter to police.
what: Pastor Frank Houston sexually abused a young boy in the 1970s. The Royal Commission's Case Study 18 findings (November 2015) found that Brian Houston and the national executive did not report the allegations to police when they emerged in 1999, and that Brian Houston had a conflict of interest as both national president and the son of the alleged perpetrator. Frank Houston died in 2004 without being charged.

title: Brian Houston acquitted of concealing father's abuse
who: Hillsong Church
network: Hillsong Church / Australian Christian Churches (Assemblies of God)
what: Hillsong founder Brian Houston was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence of another person, namely his father Frank Houston's abuse of a boy in the 1970s, which court papers said he knew of by 1999. On 17 August 2023 Magistrate Gareth Christofi found him not guilty, ruling he had a reasonable excuse for not reporting.

title: ForuM study — German Protestant Church (EKD)
who: Evangelische Kirche in Deutschland (EKD) and Diakonie
network: Evangelical Church in Germany (EKD) and Diakonie
cover_up: Researchers said regional churches delivered documents slowly despite a contract, so the study could not be completed; co-author Martin Wazlawik called the figures 'the tip of the tip of the iceberg'.
what: The ForuM study, commissioned by the EKD in 2020 and led by Hanover University of Applied Sciences and Arts, was released on 25 January 2024. Files reviewed showed 2,225 victims and 1,259 potential perpetrators among ministers, employees and volunteers since 1946, with a projected estimate of up to 9,355 abused minors. EKD head Kirsten Fehrs called it a 'massive failure' toward victims.

title: Jehovah's Witnesses — Royal Commission Case Study 29
who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Australia (Jehovah's Witnesses)
network: Jehovah's Witnesses (Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society)
cover_up: None of the 1,006 alleged perpetrators recorded since 1950 was reported to police by the church. The 'two-witness rule' required two witnesses before elders' judicial committees could act, blocking 125 allegations; 401 members were expelled after internal hearings and 230 later readmitted.
what: At hearings in July–August 2015, the Royal Commission was told the Watch Tower Society's files held 1,006 alleged perpetrators of child sexual abuse since 1950, including 579 confessions, and that none had been reported to secular authorities. The Commission referred 514 alleged perpetrators to police. Its November 2016 report found the organisation did not respond adequately to child sexual abuse and that its two-witness rule showed a serious lack of understanding of abuse.

title: Conti v. Watchtower — Fremont congregation, California
who: Watchtower Bible and Tract Society (Jehovah's Witnesses)
network: Jehovah's Witnesses (Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society)
what: In June 2012 an Alameda County jury found the Watchtower Society liable for abuse of a girl by a congregation member and awarded punitive damages, later reduced. In April 2015 the California appeals court reversed punitive damages but upheld $2.8 million in compensatory damages; the case settled during further appeal. Other US civil cases followed, including a $13.5 million San Diego judgment in 2014 (vacated 2016, settled 2018) and a $35 million Montana verdict in 2018 reversed in 2020.

title: Warren Jeffs — FLDS child 'marriages' conviction
who: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)
network: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)
what: FLDS president Warren Jeffs was added to the FBI Ten Most Wanted list on 6 May 2006 and arrested in Nevada on 28 August 2006. A 2007 Utah conviction for accomplice to rape was reversed in 2010, and Arizona charges were dismissed in 2010. In August 2011 a Texas jury convicted him of two counts of sexual assault of a child, girls aged 12 and 15 he had taken as 'spiritual wives', and he was sentenced to life plus 20 years. Texas authorities had raided the YFZ ranch on 7 April 2008 and taken custody of about 416 children, who were later returned after courts found the removal unjustified.

title: Bountiful, B.C. — parents convicted of taking 13-year-old to marry Warren Jeffs
who: FLDS, Bountiful community
network: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)
what: In February 2017 a B.C. Supreme Court judge in Cranbrook convicted Brandon James Blackmore and Emily Gail Blackmore of removing a child from Canada for sexual purposes: in 2004 they took their 13-year-old daughter to the Utah–Arizona line to be married to Warren Jeffs, then 48. Both were jailed in August 2017. In the same trial James Oler was acquitted of a related charge.

title: James Oler — removing a 15-year-old from Canada to marry
who: FLDS, Bountiful community
network: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)
what: Former FLDS Bountiful bishop James Oler was first acquitted in 2017; the B.C. Court of Appeal ordered a new trial. In May 2019 he was found guilty of removing a child from Canada, having taken a 15-year-old girl to the United States in 2004 to be married to an older FLDS member. On 29 August 2019 he was sentenced to 12 months in jail and 18 months' probation. Separately, Oler (5 wives) and Winston Blackmore (24 wives, 1990–2014) were convicted of polygamy in July 2017.

title: Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne
who: Adass Israel School (ultra-Orthodox community school)
cover_up: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. In Israel, then deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition; her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals.
what: Headmistress Malka Leifer abused pupils at Melbourne's ultra-Orthodox Adass Israel School between about 2003 and 2007. The school flew her to Israel in March 2008. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences involving at least eight pupils; she was arrested in Israel in August 2014, found in 2019 to have faked mental illness, and extradited on 25 January 2021. On 3 April 2023 a Melbourne jury found her guilty of 18 charges including rape, and in August 2023 she was sentenced to 15 years. In 2015 the Supreme Court of Victoria had ordered the school and Leifer to pay a former pupil about AU$1.27 million.

title: Yaakov Litzman — breach of trust for shielding Malka Leifer
who: Israeli Ministry of Health; ultra-Orthodox Agudat Yisrael party
cover_up: A government minister pressured ministry psychiatrists to alter evaluations of an extradition suspect.
what: Former Israeli health minister Yaakov Litzman signed a plea deal in January 2022 admitting breach of trust for pressuring Health Ministry employees to change psychiatric evaluations so that Malka Leifer would appear unfit to stand extradition trial. He resigned from the Knesset in June 2022 and on 8 August 2022 the Jerusalem Magistrate's Court sentenced him to eight months' probation and a fine of about US$900. Australian Jewish groups condemned the deal as lenient.

title: Charity Commission inquiry — Manchester New Moston Jehovah's Witnesses congregation
who: Manchester New Moston Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses (charity); Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain
network: Jehovah's Witnesses (Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society)
cover_up: Trustees dismissed one allegation as a matter between two teenagers, did not enforce restrictions on the accused, and the victims were effectively required to repeat their allegations at an internal hearing in front of the abuser, who was allowed to question them. The charity did not give the Commission accurate and complete answers. The Watch Tower Society fought the inquiry through five courts a
what: Allegations of child abuse against a trustee of the New Moston congregation were made in 2012 and 2013; he was later convicted of two counts of indecent assault. The Charity Commission opened a statutory inquiry on 27 May 2014 and published its report on 26 July 2017, finding the trustees had not adequately dealt with the allegations. The Commission also ran a wider inquiry into the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain.

title: A v Watchtower — High Court damages over Peter Stewart abuse
who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain
network: Jehovah's Witnesses (Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society)
what: On 19 June 2015 the High Court (A v Watchtower Bible and Tract Society [2015] EWHC 1722 (QB)) awarded £275,000 damages to a woman abused as a child by Jehovah's Witness ministerial servant Peter Stewart, holding the organisation liable. Separately, in July 2014 Barry congregation elder Mark Sewell was found guilty of eight sex offences including rape and sentenced to 14 years; a church judicial committee had earlier cleared him after the women reported him, and victims said other elders told them not to 'gossip' about the attacks.

title: Utrecht University / WODC study — Jehovah's Witnesses in the Netherlands
who: Jehovah's Witnesses (Netherlands)
network: Jehovah's Witnesses (Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society)
what: A study by Utrecht University researchers led by Kees van den Bos, commissioned by the Ministry of Justice's research centre WODC, was published on 23 January 2020. 751 participants reported experiences; only 27% of cases led to a police report. Victims were critical of internal handling by elders; the researchers recommended better support, elder training, an internal reporting centre, and that lawmakers consider a duty to report abuse to police.

title: Pennsylvania grand jury — Jehovah's Witnesses child sexual abuse charges
who: Jehovah's Witnesses congregations in Pennsylvania
network: Jehovah's Witnesses (Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society)
what: A statewide investigating grand jury in Harrisburg, opened after a county prosecutor's referral, heard dozens of witnesses about abuse in Jehovah's Witness congregations. On 7 July 2023 Attorney General Michelle Henry announced charges against five more men, bringing the total to 14 charged; one earlier suspect killed himself before arrest. One former elder was later convicted in Lancaster County.

title: Latter-day Saints abuse help line — Bisbee, Arizona case (AP investigation)
who: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
network: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
cover_up: After the father confessed to his bishop, the bishop called the church's abuse help line; church lawyers told him the clergy-penitent privilege meant he had to keep it secret. AP reported the abuse continued for about seven years afterwards. The help line, set up in 1995, routes calls that pose legal risk to church attorneys.
what: Paul Douglas Adams, a Border Patrol employee and church member in Bisbee, abused his daughter from age 5 and later a second daughter, and filmed the abuse; he stopped only when arrested in 2017 and died by suicide in jail before trial. An AP investigation published 4 August 2022 found church officials had known for years through confessions. Arizona law, like more than 20 states, lets clergy withhold abuse learned in confession. The church disputed the AP's account.

title: Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad
who: German Foreign Office; Colonia Dignidad
cover_up: Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said in April 2016 that 'over the course of many years, from the 60s to the 80s, German diplomats at best looked away' and that the embassy failed to shield Germans at the colony.
what: In April 2016 Germany released Foreign Office files from 1986–1996 and the foreign minister admitted diplomats had failed colony residents, including abused children. In 2017 the Bundestag formally acknowledged German responsibility and asked the government to plan an investigation, memorial and help for victims; in 2019 Germany announced compensation payments to victims.

title: Re ST (A Minor) — High Court judgment on The Family (Children of God)
who: The Family / Children of God (now The Family International)
what: In a custody case in the High Court Family Division, Lord Justice Alan Ward gave judgment in chambers on 26 May 1995 and handed it down publicly on 19 October 1995. He found that a high proportion of children in The Family were exposed to adult sexual activity and that a significant number had sexual activity forced on them by adults, and he described harsh discipline including silence restriction and exorcisms of children. He found the group had made changes he judged likely to be irreversible, let the mother keep custody on conditions, required the group to ban corporal punishment of children in the UK by anyone other than parents, and said it must denounce founder David Berg and acknowledge that through his writings he was personally responsible for children being subjected to sexually inappropriate behaviour.

title: Argentina raids on The Family (Children of God) communes
who: The Family / Children of God
what: On 1 September 1993 Judge Roberto Marquevich ordered raids on Family communes near Buenos Aires; 137 children were taken into state custody and about 30 members arrested. The judge said nine children showed signs of 'cruel and atrocious maltreatment', which the group disputed. Children were later released after examination and no convictions resulted. Raids in Australia (1992, including Panton Hill, Victoria), France and Spain also ended without convictions.

title: Twelve Tribes — Bavaria child removals upheld by European Court
who: Twelve Tribes (Zwölf Stämme)
what: On 5 September 2013 more than 100 Bavarian police removed 40 children from two Twelve Tribes communities after undercover recordings by journalist Wolfram Kuhnigk showed children being beaten with rods; the group says it canes disobedient children. This was physical, not sexual, abuse; the children were placed in foster care. In 2018 the European Court of Human Rights (Wetjen and Others v. Germany) upheld the removals because of the risk of inhuman or degrading treatment.

title: NXIVM — Keith Raniere convicted (including sexual exploitation of a 15-year-old)
who: NXIVM (self-help group run as a cult)
what: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted NXIVM leader Keith Raniere in June 2019 of racketeering, racketeering conspiracy, sex trafficking, attempted sex trafficking, forced labour conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy. Prosecutors proved as racketeering acts that at 45 he sexually exploited a 15-year-old girl and photographed the abuse. On 27 October 2020 he was sentenced to 120 years and fined $1.75 million.

title: Tony Alamo Christian Ministries — leader convicted of transporting girls across state lines
who: Tony Alamo Christian Ministries
what: On 24 July 2009 a federal jury convicted Tony Alamo on all 10 counts of transporting minors across state lines for sex; women testified he had taken them as 'wives' when they were children, some as young as 9. On 13 November 2009 he was sentenced to 175 years and fined $250,000. In 2013 federal authorities moved against 27 properties held by members to collect $2.5 million restitution. He died in custody in 2017.

title: Agape Boarding School — Christian boys' school, Missouri
who: Agape Boarding School (independent Baptist ministry)
cover_up: The state Attorney General's office said 22 workers should have been charged with serious crimes, but the county prosecutor charged five with low-level counts; in Missouri only the local prosecutor can file charges.
what: Former students came forward in 2020. In 2021 the school's longtime doctor, David Smock, was charged with child sex crimes and five staff with low-level abuse counts; two later pleaded guilty to misdemeanours. Missouri passed a 2021 law tightening oversight of religious boarding schools. Agape closed on 20 January 2023.

title: Royal Commission Case Study 22 — Yeshivah Melbourne and Yeshiva Bondi
who: Yeshivah Centre / Chabad Institutions of Victoria; Yeshiva Centre – Chabad NSW
network: Yeshivah Centre Melbourne and Yeshiva Centre Bondi (Chabad)
cover_up: The Commission found that the principle of mesirah (not informing on a fellow Jew to secular authorities) as applied in the community discouraged reporting, and survivors who went to police were treated as outcasts. Bondi's Rabbi Yossi Feldman testified he 'was not aware it was illegal to touch a child's genitals'; the Commission found him ignorant of the duty to report.
what: The Royal Commission held hearings in February 2015 on responses to abuse by David Cyprys, David Kramer and Aron Kestecher at Yeshivah Melbourne and Daniel Hayman at Yeshiva Bondi. Its report (released October–November 2016) found 'a marked absence of supportive leadership' for survivors at Yeshivah Melbourne. Its 2017 final report recommended Jewish institutions state that mesirah does not apply to reporting child sexual abuse.

title: Nechemya Weberman — Satmar counsellor, Williamsburg
who: Satmar Hasidic community, Brooklyn
cover_up: During the case men were arrested for trying to bribe the victim and her husband to drop it; four were later convicted of coercion or witness tampering. Others photographed her on the witness stand and posted the images online.
what: Nechemya Weberman, an unlicensed counsellor in the Satmar community, abused a girl from age 12 to 15. He was convicted on all 59 counts on 10 December 2012 and sentenced on 22 January 2013 to 103 years, later cut on appeal. Brooklyn DA figures showed about 100 of 5,389 sex abuse cases since 2009 came from the Haredi community; critics said DA Charles Hynes's policy of not naming Haredi defendants protected the community.

title: AP investigation — sexual abuse in Pakistan's madrassas
who: Islamic seminaries (madrassas), over 22,000 registered with at least 2 million pupils
cover_up: Police are often paid off and refuse to register cases; families of poor victims are pressured to 'forgive' clerics and accept money, which Pakistani law allows; the religious affairs minister dismissed the claims. Police told AP that clerics are almost never convicted.
what: An AP investigation published 21 November 2017 found sexual abuse by clerics was pervasive in Pakistan's madrassas and seldom prosecuted. In one case a 9-year-old's teacher confessed but was freed after the mother 'forgave' him for $300. A follow-up AP investigation in 2020, based on dozens of police reports, found the same pattern.

title: Herry Wirawan — Islamic boarding school, Bandung
who: Islamic boarding schools (pesantren) run by the offender
what: Herry Wirawan, head of Islamic boarding schools near Bandung, raped 13 girl students aged 12 to 16 between 2016 and 2021, making eight pregnant. A Bandung court gave him life in prison in February 2022; on prosecutors' appeal the Bandung High Court sentenced him to death on 4 April 2022.

title: Asaram Bapu — convicted of raping a 16-year-old at his ashram
who: Asaram Bapu ashrams
cover_up: Witnesses in his cases were attacked; a former aide was shot dead in May 2014 and the key witness in the Surat case was shot dead in January 2015.
what: A 16-year-old girl said guru Asaram Bapu assaulted her on 15 August 2013 at his Manai ashram; he was arrested by Jodhpur police on 1 September 2013. On 25 April 2018 a Jodhpur court convicted him of raping a minor and sentenced him to life imprisonment. In January 2023 a Gandhinagar court gave him a second life term in a case brought by two sisters from Surat.

title: Nithyananda — Gujarat abduction case and flight from India
who: Nithyananda Dhyanapeetam
what: In November 2019 Gujarat Police arrested two of Nithyananda's disciples on charges of kidnapping, wrongful confinement and using children to collect donations at his Ahmedabad ashram, after a Bengaluru couple said their daughters were being held there; two children aged 9 and 10 told police they had been tortured, made to work and confined. Police said on 21 November 2019 that Nithyananda had fled India after a rape case was registered against him in Karnataka. He later claimed to have founded a 'Hindu nation', Kailasa. A Gujarat High Court plea by the parents over their adult daughters was rejected.

title: Manitoba Colony 'ghost rapes' — Mennonite colony, Bolivia
who: Old Colony Mennonite community, Manitoba Colony
cover_up: The attacks were first blamed on ghosts or demons; a 2013 investigation reported similar assaults continuing.
what: Men from the Manitoba Mennonite Colony sprayed a drug through bedroom windows to sedate households, then broke in and raped women and girls, including small children. The attacks came to light in June 2009. In August 2011 a Bolivian court convicted the men of raping and sexually assaulting 151 women and girls; seven were sentenced to 25 years and an eighth man got 12 years for supplying the drug.

title: Royal Commission data — Uniting Church in Australia
who: Uniting Church in Australia
what: At a Royal Commission hearing on 10 March 2017, the Uniting Church was reported to have faced about 2,500 allegations of child sexual abuse over its 40-year history (it was formed in 1977). The Commission's Case Study 23 also examined Knox Grammar School, a Uniting Church school in Sydney.

title: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane — Archbishop Peter Hollingworth's handling of abuse
who: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane; Toowoomba Preparatory School; Church of England Boys' Society
cover_up: A diocesan inquiry found that in 1993 Archbishop Hollingworth allowed a known paedophile to keep working as a priest. He later became Governor-General of Australia.
what: Peter Hollingworth was Anglican Archbishop of Brisbane from 1989 to 2001 and became Governor-General in June 2001. In December 2001 he faced allegations that he had handled sexual abuse cases poorly as archbishop. His successor, Phillip Aspinall, set up a church inquiry in February 2002 into the handling of nine abuse cases; its report was tabled in the Queensland Parliament on 1 May 2003, and Aspinall said Hollingworth had made a 'grave and serious' error of judgement. Hollingworth announced his resignation as Governor-General on 25 May 2003.

title: Salvation Army boys' homes — Australia
who: The Salvation Army (Australia)
cover_up: The Royal Commission heard that officers accused of abuse were moved interstate.
what: The Salvation Army sheltered about 30,000 Australian children from the 1940s to the 1980s and apologised in 2006 for abuse that may have occurred. Private settlements totalling A$15.5 million for 474 cases in Victoria were reported in 2013. In January–February 2014 the Royal Commission's Case Study 5 examined abuse at Bexley Boys' Home, Gill Memorial Home (Goulburn), Alkira (Indooroopilly) and Riverview Training Farm, and how accused officers were investigated and transferred.

title: Rev. Gordon Nakayama — Anglican dioceses of New Westminster and Calgary
who: Anglican Church of Canada; Japanese Canadian congregations
cover_up: Nakayama made a written confession in 1994; the dioceses did not report it to police. He was allowed to resign and died in 1995.
what: Gordon Goichi Nakayama served for more than 50 years as an Anglican priest to Japanese Canadian communities in the dioceses of Calgary and New Westminster. In 1994 he admitted a history of sexually abusing minors and shortly before his death in 1995 signed a written confession to Archbishop Barry Curtis; he was charged with immorality under church law and resigned from ministry, but police were not told. On 15 June 2015 the two dioceses formally apologised to survivors in Vancouver. The church said it is not known how many minors were abused.

title: Terry Knight — Diocese of Portsmouth
who: Church of England, Diocese of Portsmouth
cover_up: Bishop Timothy Bavin did not report Knight to police when parents raised concerns in 1985.
what: Terry Knight, active in the Diocese of Portsmouth, was convicted of child sexual offences in 1996 and again in 2016. Parents had raised concerns with the bishop in 1985, who did not inform police.

title: Dilworth School — Anglican boarding school, Auckland
who: Dilworth Trust (Anglican-linked school for boys from disadvantaged families)
cover_up: The independent inquiry concluded that ongoing silence about the abuse was 'the primary reason for the damage' to former students.
what: Police arrested and charged six men on 14 September 2020 over offences at Dilworth alleged to date from the 1970s to the early 2000s. An independent inquiry led by Dame Silvia Cartwright and Frances Joychild KC, released on 18 September 2023 and covering 1950 to the present, found that sexual abuse was committed consistently from the mid-1950s to the end of 2005: 126 of 171 former students who gave information reported being sexually abused, and the inquiry knew of 49 more. Police estimated 233 student victims. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care also examined Dilworth.

title: Gloriavale Christian Community — convictions and Employment Court findings
who: Gloriavale Christian Community
cover_up: In January 2025 Gloriavale's leadership said past leaders had not reported known abuse to authorities; in 2026 the Charities Registration Board cited the school's failure to report child sexual offending.
what: Founder Neville Cooper ('Hopeful Christian') was sentenced in December 1995 to five years in prison on three charges of indecent assault against a young woman, after an earlier conviction on 10 counts involving five young complainants was overturned on appeal. In May 2022 the Employment Court ruled that three former members had been employees from age six, doing 'strenuous, difficult and sometimes dangerous' work. Leader Howard Temple pleaded guilty in 2025 to indecently assaulting six girls and young women between 2002 and 2022, resigned as leader, and on 12 December 2025 was jailed for 26 months.

title: Jesus Fellowship (Jesus Army) — Operation Lifeboat and redress scheme
who: Jesus Fellowship Church / Jesus Fellowship Community Trust
what: After founder Noel Stanton died in 2009, Northamptonshire Police ran Operation Lifeboat into historic abuse; about ten to twelve former members were convicted of sex offences. The church's redress scheme, whose final report was published on 11 September 2024, received 601 applications, paid £7.7 million, identified 539 alleged perpetrators and accepted responsibility for 264 of them, 61% of whom were former leaders.

title: Independent Fundamental Baptist churches — Star-Telegram investigation
who: Independent Fundamental Baptist churches and institutions
what: A Fort Worth Star-Telegram investigation published in December 2018 identified 412 allegations of sexual misconduct in 187 Independent Fundamental Baptist churches and institutions across 40 US states and Canada, some dating back to the 1970s. Reporters spoke to more than 200 current or former members, and described accused men being able to move to other churches through informal networks of church-college alumni.

title: Jack Schaap — First Baptist Church of Hammond, Indiana
who: First Baptist Church of Hammond / Hyles-Anderson College (IFB)
what: Jack Schaap, pastor of the 15,000-member First Baptist Church of Hammond, was fired in July 2012 after admitting a sexual relationship with a 16-year-old girl from the church. He pleaded guilty to taking a minor across state lines with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity and on 20 March 2013 was sentenced to 12 years in federal prison. Earlier, church deacon A.V. Ballenger was sentenced in 1993 for molesting a child.

title: Samuel Bateman — FLDS splinter group, Short Creek
who: Splinter group of the FLDS led by Samuel Bateman
network: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)
what: Samuel Bateman began claiming to be a new prophet in 2019 and led a group that broke off from the FLDS church. In a plea agreement he admitted 'spiritually marrying' 20 women and girls, 10 of them under age, with the intent of sexual activity with the girls. He was arrested in 2022, when nine child 'brides' were removed from homes. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transport a minor for criminal sexual activity and conspiracy to commit kidnapping, and on 9 December 2024 a federal judge in Phoenix sentenced him to 50 years. Two male followers who went to trial were convicted.

title: La Luz del Mundo — leader Naasón Joaquín García convicted
who: La Luz del Mundo church (HQ Guadalajara, Mexico)
what: Naasón Joaquín García, leader of La Luz del Mundo, was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport on 3 June 2019 on charges brought by the California Attorney General including forcible rape of a minor, production of child pornography and human trafficking. On 3 June 2022, days before trial, he pleaded guilty to three counts involving minors (two of forcible oral copulation and one lewd act on a 15-year-old), and on 8 June 2022 was sentenced to more than 16 years in prison. Co-defendant Alondra Ocampo pleaded guilty to four counts in 2020. In October 2023 a federal grand jury indicted him for producing and possessing child pornography involving a 16-year-old follower.

title: Apollo Quiboloy — Kingdom of Jesus Christ
who: Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC)
what: A federal grand jury in the Central District of California returned a 42-count superseding indictment on 10 November 2021 (unsealed 18 November) charging Quiboloy and eight church administrators, including with sex trafficking of children. It alleges females aged about 12 to 25 were recruited as personal assistants and required to have sex with him, and that church members were brought to the US on fraudulently obtained visas and forced to solicit donations for a sham charity. In 2024 the Philippine Department of Justice charged him with sexual abuse and a court ordered his arrest; after a two-week police operation at the church's Davao City compound he surrendered and was taken into custody on 8 September 2024. He denies the charges.

title: Global Ikhwan (GISB) children's homes — Operation Global
who: Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB), linked to the banned Al-Arqam movement
network: Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB)
what: On 11 September 2024 Malaysian police raided 20 charity homes linked to GISB Holdings in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, rescued 402 children aged 1 to 17 and arrested 171 adults, after six months of intelligence work; police said they had received 41 reports about the group since 2011. By 10 October police put the total rescued at 625. Three madrasah student assistants in Kuala Pilah were charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing five children in 2022–2023, another teaching assistant with sexually assaulting four boys, and others with physical abuse of children; police said the investigation pointed to organised crime and human trafficking.

title: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
what: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.

title: Lev Tahor — Guatemala removal of 160 minors
who: Lev Tahor
what: In December 2024 Guatemalan authorities removed 160 children from a Lev Tahor property in Oratorio, Santa Rosa, where the group had settled in 2016, after four minors escaped and reported abuse; the group was accused of sexual violence against minors and human trafficking. Members later forced their way into a shelter and tried to take back children. The group had earlier left the United States and Canada for Mexico and Guatemala.

title: ISKCON boarding schools (gurukulas) — acknowledged abuse
who: International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON)
what: In the 1990s ISKCON leaders acknowledged physical, emotional and sexual abuse of children in the movement's boarding schools in the US and India in the 1970s and 1980s, and in 1998 ISKCON itself published an exposé. A $900 million lawsuit filed in Texas in 2002 (the Turley case) led ISKCON temples into Chapter 11 bankruptcy and a $15 million settlement in 2008. ISKCON then set up a Child Protection Office.

title: Mamou Alliance Academy — missionary children's boarding school, Guinea
who: Christian and Missionary Alliance (C&MA)
cover_up: Alumni wrote to C&MA headquarters about abuse from the 1980s for about ten years before an inquiry was set up.
what: Mamou Alliance Academy boarded the children of C&MA missionaries in West Africa. After 30 alumni asked for an investigation in 1995, an independent commission of inquiry heard 80 testimonies and reported in April 1998 that the denomination had been negligent; it identified nine offenders, and abuse included sexual molestation and rape. The US C&MA board issued an open letter asking victims' forgiveness.

title: New Tribes Mission — Fanda boarding school, Senegal
who: New Tribes Mission (now Ethnos360)
what: A 2010 report by GRACE (Godly Response to Abuse in the Christian Environment), commissioned by New Tribes Mission after pressure from survivors, accused the mission of a culture of systemic abuse at the Fanda boarding school it ran in Senegal for missionaries' children, including sexual abuse of more than 20 children; a former dorm parent was identified as the most prolific perpetrator. 1992 field committee notes said allegations should not be reported to police. The mission then set up its own investigation process, IHART, to examine historical allegations at other schools.

title: New Tribes Mission missionary convicted of abusing Katukina girls in Brazil
who: New Tribes Mission
what: Missionary Warren Scott Kennell, who was trying to set up a church among the Katukina people in Brazil, was arrested in May 2013 on arrival at Orlando airport after a tip that he had posted abuse images online. Investigators found more than 940 child abuse images on his computer; he admitted abusing a girl shown in one and photographing a second. He pleaded guilty to two counts of producing child abuse images and was sentenced in 2014 to 58 years in federal prison.

title: Trokosi — ritual servitude of girls at shrines
who: Traditional shrines (Ewe in Ghana and Togo; Fon in Benin)
what: Under trokosi, shrines take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing; they serve priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty, which defenders deny. Ghana amended its Criminal Code in 1998 to make ritual or customary servitude a crime with a minimum three-year sentence, but the practice continued and no prosecutions are recorded in the source.

title: Devadasi dedication of girls — Karnataka and neighbouring states
who: Temple dedication practice (mostly Dalit girls)
what: Girls, mostly from Dalit families, are dedicated to temple deities and then sexually exploited, despite laws against the practice, including Karnataka's 1982 ban. The Karnataka government's last survey, in 2008, counted 40,600 devadasis; NGOs and a 2018 Karnataka State Women's University study found more than 80,000. Girls as young as seven have been pushed into the tradition.
